title: Guess Number Higher or Lower II
statement:
A secret integer has been chosen somewhere in the range 1 to `n`, and you find it by guessing. A correct guess ends the game at no cost. A wrong guess `x` costs you `x` dollars, and you are then told whether the secret is larger or smaller than `x`, so you can keep guessing.

Return the least amount of money you must hold so that, playing the best strategy, you are certain to find the secret no matter which number was chosen (that is, the smallest possible worst-case total you can be charged).
notes:
## Intuition

You do not get to pick which secret is chosen, so think of an opponent who always answers in the way that costs you most. Each guess splits the range into a part below and a part above it, and the opponent sends you into whichever part is more expensive. Trying every guessing tree directly explodes, but the cost of a range depends only on its two ends, so there are just O(n²) ranges to solve, and each one can be built from shorter ranges.

## Approach

1. Let `dp[low][high]` be the money needed to guarantee a win when the secret lies in `low..high`. A range of one number (or an empty one) costs `0`, which the zero-filled table already holds.
2. Solve ranges in order of increasing `length`, so both halves of a split are ready.
3. For a range `low..high`, try every `guess`. If it is wrong you pay `guess` and then face the worse half: `worst = guess + max(dp[low][guess - 1], dp[guess + 1][high])`.
4. Keep the smallest `worst` as `best` and store it in `dp[low][high]`.
5. Return `dp[1][n]`.

## Example 1, step by step

For `n = 10`, ranges of length 2 cost their smaller number (`dp[8][9] = 8`, `dp[9][10] = 9`), and ranges of length 3 cost their middle number (`dp[8][10] = 9`). Building up, `dp[1][6] = 8`. For the full range, `guess = 7` gives `7 + max(dp[1][6], dp[8][10]) = 7 + max(8, 9) = 16`, and no other guess does better (for example `guess = 6` gives `6 + max(6, 16) = 22`), so the answer is `16`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³): O(n²) ranges, each trying up to n guesses.
- Space: O(n²) for the table.

## Pitfalls

- This is minimax, not binary search: guessing the middle is not always optimal (for `n = 10` the best first guess is 7, not 5).
- A correct guess is free; only wrong guesses are charged, so a single-number range costs `0`.
- Size the table `n + 2` so `dp[guess + 1][high]` with `guess = high` and `dp[low][guess - 1]` with `guess = low` read a zero instead of falling off the edge.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `dp[low][high]` | money that guarantees a win when the secret is in `low..high` |
| `length` | size of the ranges being solved in this round |
| `low`, `high` | the two ends of the current range |
| `guess` | the number tried first in that range |
| `worst` | cost if `guess` is wrong and the opponent picks the worse half |
| `best` | the smallest `worst` over all guesses so far |

narration.2: Build a zero-filled table; dp[low][high] will hold the cost of guaranteeing a win in low..high, and ranges of one number cost nothing.
narration.3: Solve ranges from short to long so every smaller range is ready when it is needed.
narration.4: Slide a range of the current length across 1..n by its left end.
narration.5: The right end follows from the left end and the length.
narration.6: No guess has been tried yet for this range.
narration.7: Try every number in the range as the first guess.
narration.8: If the guess is wrong we pay it, and the opponent sends us into the more expensive side.
narration.9: Keep the cheapest worst case among the guesses.
narration.11: Store the cost of this range for longer ranges to use.
narration.14: The whole range 1..n is the answer.
